_note: Italian pronunciation drills by first language, for /culture/mistakes and the Aussprache-Check. Each drill practises one Italian sound or pattern that is hard from a particular first language (transfer, see fehler-nach-sprache.json). `pairs`: minimal pairs, the first word is the target, the second is what often comes out instead or a word to tell it apart from; both are real Italian words (e/è, ho/o and a few accent pairs are the same sounds written differently). `words`: practice words without a partner. `sentence`: to repeat, scored like the Aussprache-Check; it contains one word of every pair. `fehler`: the ids of the mistakes in fehler-nach-sprache.json that this drill practises (the other side of their `drill`; checked by pnpm check:aussprache). Standard Italian; the file's `variety` covers every drill and `regional` (optional) says where speech differs in daily life. Drill ids that still fit kept their slot id (h, r, nasal, u, betonung, aspiration), the rest are new (content-plan §5.6). Languages: English, German, French, Portuguese and Spanish speakers (the five first languages of the plan). Arabic, Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese drills of the Spanish course were removed, not translated. Audio: public/audio/muttersprache/<slug>.mp3 once it-IT recordings exist; until then the browser voice reads them.

doppie.title: Single or double consonant?
doppie.tip: A written double consonant is long: hold it about twice as long as a single one, and keep the vowel before it short. It changes the word: sete is thirst, sette is seven. English does it between words (“black cat”), but never inside one. For p, t, c, b, d, g hold the closure silently, then release.
doppie.sentence: Mio nonno ha sete: compra una cassa d'acqua e un cappello.

vocali.title: Clear vowels, also at the end
vocali.tip: Italian vowels stay short, pure and full in every syllable, stressed or not, and the last vowel of a word is always said. No gliding (not “beh-nay”), no weak “uh”, no silent final e. The last vowel often carries the meaning: casa (house), case (houses); gatto (tomcat), gatta (cat).
vocali.sentence: Il mio amico ha una casa e un gatto.

e-o.title: Open and closed e
e-o.tip: In a stressed syllable, e has an open sound /ɛ/ (like “bed”) and a closed sound /e/ (like “eh” without gliding). The accent shows it on a last syllable: è (is) is open, perché is closed. e (and) has no accent and is short. Listen first, then copy the word you hear. Regional speech varies, so no one expects it perfect.
e-o.sentence: Il caffè è caldo e il tè è buono.

r.title: r or rr?
r.tip: A single r is one quick tap of the tongue tip behind your top teeth. rr is a trill, several quick taps. Say “caro” fast, then keep the tongue moving for “carro”. The r at the start of a word is a trill too. Neither one comes from the throat.
r.sentence: Era sera: il carro rosso non era caro.

c-g.title: c and g: soft or hard?
c-g.tip: Before e and i, c is like ch in “church” and g is like j in “jam”: cena, gelato. With an h they turn hard: che and chi start with a k, ghetto with a hard g. Never “church” for chi, and never a rasp or th for ce. A silent i keeps the soft sound before a, o, u: ciao, giorno.
c-g.sentence: Chi ci porta a fare un giro? Che bello!

sc.title: sc and sch
sc.tip: Before e or i, sc is like sh in “ship”: scena, sci, pesce. Before a, o, u, and in sche and schi, it is s + k: scala, scuola, scheda, schiena. The h in sch keeps it a k. Between vowels the sh is long: pesce, lascia.
sc.sentence: Dopo la scuola vado a sciare, ma mi fa male la schiena.

gn-gl.title: gn and gli
gn-gl.tip: gn is one sound, like ny in “canyon”. gli is one sound too, like lli in “million”, but longer. Press the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth for both. Don't say g + n or g + l, and don't say a plain n or l: figlio is not filo.
gn-gl.sentence: Mio figlio ha un sogno: fare il bagno ogni giorno in famiglia.

regional.note: In the north zero, mezzo and pranzo have a voiced dz; in the centre and south the same words often have ts. Both are normal.

z.title: z: ts or dz
z.tip: Italian z is two sounds in one: the tongue starts at your top teeth and the air comes out as a hiss, either unvoiced (ts, as in “cats”: zio, grazie) or voiced (dz, as in “beds”: zero). It is never a plain buzzing z, never th, and never just s. -zione is always ts. Double zz is long: pizza.
z.sentence: Posso mangiare la pizza con lo zio a pranzo, grazie?

regional.note: Between vowels, s is voiced in the north (casa, museo) and voiceless in the south. Both are normal; the drill uses the standard rules.

s.title: s: sharp or voiced
s.tip: Before b, d, g, l, m, n, r and v, s is voiced, like z in “zoo”: sbaglio, smettere, sveglia. Before a vowel at the start of a word and before p, t, c, f, q it is sharp, as in “sun”: sole, sport, scuola. Put a finger on your throat: it should buzz on sm- and sb-.
s.sentence: Smetto di lavorare e vado a casa con una rosa.

b-v.title: b or v?
b-v.tip: b and v are two different sounds in Italian. For b both lips close. For v the top teeth touch your lower lip and the air keeps flowing. Put your finger on your throat: both are voiced. bene (well) and vene (veins) are different words.
b-v.sentence: Vivo bene in una valle vicino a Verona e bevo vino.

qu.title: qu: say the u
qu.tip: In Italian qu is k + w, as in “quick”: you say the u. quando is “KWAN-do”, not “KAN-do”, and questo is “KWE-sto”. This is different from Spanish and French, where the u of que and qui is silent.
qu.sentence: Quanto costa questo quaderno? Quattro euro.

aspiration.title: p, t, k without a puff
aspiration.tip: Italian p, t and k come with no puff of air. Hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth: it should hardly move. t and d touch the back of your top teeth. Start the vowel straight away.
aspiration.sentence: Prendo un tè e un caffè con pane e tanto burro.

h.title: h is silent
h.tip: Never say the letter h: ho sounds just like o, and hanno sounds just like anno. Start straight on the next vowel and don't breathe out first. The h only keeps ho, hai, ha, hanno apart from o, ai, a, anno.
h.sentence: Ho fame e hanno fame anche loro.

st-sp.title: s before a consonant
st-sp.tip: A word can start with s + p, t, c, b or d, and there is no vowel in front of it. Start on a clean s: scuola, studente, sbaglio. Not “escuola”, not “sh” as in “shtudente”, and don't add an “e” after it either.
st-sp.sentence: Lo studente spagnolo fa la spesa in una strada vicino alla stazione.

nasal.title: Vowel, then a real n
nasal.tip: Say the vowel clean, with no air through your nose, and then close it with a real n or m. Italian has no nasal vowels: pane is “pa” + “ne”, and you feel your tongue touch behind your teeth for the n. Before c and g the n is made at the back of the mouth: anche, lungo.
nasal.sentence: Il bambino mangia un po' di pane con cinque amici.

u.title: u, always round and back
u.tip: Italian u is the French “ou” (vous) and the u of “moon”. Round your lips and pull your tongue back. It is never the French u of “tu” or the German ü. Italian tu and French tu are two different sounds.
u.sentence: Lunedì tu hai una cena con Luca e Lucia.

ti-di.title: t and d before i
ti-di.tip: In Italian t and d stay plain before i: tipo is “TEE-po”, not “CHEE-po”, and dire is “DEE-re”, not “JEE-re”. Touch the back of your top teeth with the tongue tip, release and go straight to the vowel.

betonung.title: Stress and written accents
betonung.tip: Most Italian words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable. A word stressed on its last syllable has a written accent: città, caffè, papà. The stress is almost never written inside a word, so learn it with the word. A few words change with it: papa (the Pope) and papà (dad); subito (immediately) and subìto (suffered).
betonung.sentence: Papà ha un telefono e chiama subito, ma ancora non risponde.
